04 / SUPPRESS

Controlling fire.
Understanding how.

Compare cooling with methods that influence the movement of gas around a flame.

FLEX / FLAME EXTINCTION RESEARCH

What makes combustion stop?

A flame needs a continuing supply of fuel and oxygen, along with enough heat to sustain its reactions. In FLEX, researchers studied liquid fuel droplets and tested suppression through dilution of the surrounding atmosphere with carbon dioxide and helium. These experiments help identify conditions under which a flame can no longer sustain itself.

WHAT WAS VARIED

The surrounding gas mixture

Adding a diluent changes the atmosphere around the droplet. The response depends on the gas mixture and fuel; carbon dioxide and helium should not be treated as interchangeable simply because both can suppress a flame.

WHAT TO COMPARE

Fuel, size and atmosphere

To compare extinction results, first match the fuel, initial droplet size, pressure and gas concentrations. A droplet experiment does not directly establish how an installed solid material will burn or be extinguished.

WHAT TO CHECK NEXT

Whether reactions continue

Under suitable conditions, cool-flame chemistry can persist after a visible hot flame disappears. The cool-flame sequence in Understand explains this distinction. A disappearing bright flame alone does not demonstrate that combustion has stopped.

Three approaches to suppression.

MECHANISM EXPLORER

Mechanisms are illustrated without predicting extinguishment, discharge settings or safe conditions. Ionic and acoustic techniques are research approaches, not established substitutes for spacecraft extinguishers.

01 / COOLING

Fine water mist

Small water droplets have a large total surface area relative to their volume. As the droplets heat and evaporate, they absorb energy from the surroundings. This helps cool the combustion region. Steam can also dilute the gases around the flame.

A gas-driven delivery system can discharge mist in different orientations without relying on gravity to feed water into the outlet.

NASA: fine-water-mist design ↗
02 / GAS MOTION

Electric-field-driven ionic wind

Ionic wind occurs when ions move through an electric field and transfer momentum to neutral gas molecules through collisions. The resulting gas motion can influence flame shape, heat transfer and stability without a mechanical fan.

The effect depends on the configuration: changing airflow does not necessarily extinguish a flame. NASA’s E-FIELD Flames investigation studied this interaction.

NASA: E-FIELD Flames ↗
03 / OSCILLATING FLOW

Acoustic fire suppression

Sound-driven disturbances can move gases and alter a flame. Acoustic fire suppression remains experimental. The illustration shows oscillating gas motion rather than selective removal of oxygen molecules.

A disturbance may weaken a flame or change its burning behaviour. Without sufficient cooling, disappearance of the visible flame does not establish that the fuel is safe from reignition.
